title: How The Evolution Of AI Could Impact The Future Existence Of Marketing Executives
text:
Thought leaders from around the world gathered at the Zeta Live conference in New York City, and a key topic was what the role of the chief marketing officer (CMO) would be in the future. While most conference panel speakers were confident that the position would still be around for most companies, the skills and priorities will change thanks mainly to the advancement of AI and other sources of technology. Digital marketing has the potential to become a highly personalized, productive and prosperous endeavor.
Intelligence Is The Future
“The future is not artificial intelligence, but just intelligence,” said John Sculley, co-founder, vice-chairman and director of Zeta Global, at the opening discussion. A highly acclaimed expert on technology and consumerism, Sculley was formerly president of PepsiCo
Actions Created From Real-Time Analytics
“We, as marketers, need to pair listening with actions,” explained Nicole Phillips, CMO of CVS Caremark, the online pharmacy service provided by CVS. Phillips discussed how listening to real-time feedback from users of its services is critical to delivering increasingly better experiences. Other consumer feedback comes from surveys and social listening, or what is more commonly referred to as sentiment analysis. “We have over 200,000 employees that also provide critical feedback based on customer interactions. We need to synthesize all of this feedback and data, then create actions that help us build a stronger consumer experience,” said Phillips.
Marketers Need To Work With AI Or Be Left Behind
Using AI-based tools can help collect data in real-time and create higher levels of efficiency by analyzing data at scale, improving business processes. Assisted AI can help refine and improve products and services, and AI can help develop new growth areas. However, human intelligence is still needed to guide AI technologies. Unlike humans, AI lacks conscious intentions and cannot use subjective reasoning. Not to mention, AI is not culturally sensitive. Marketers need to work alongside various forms of intelligence, including AI. “Not using AI will put you at a disadvantage,” said Ramon Jones, executive vice president and CMO of Nationwide.
Quantum Marketing
Almost everything about marketing will need to be reimagined over the next few years, including how AI and other technologies are used and explored. While the CMO job may not become extinct, the role we know today will vastly differ. In Raja Rajamannar’s book Quantum Marketing, he likens the future of marketing to quantum physics. He talks about how the principles of physics and the world we live in can be applied to the future of marketing. Rajamannar is the chief marketing and communications officer of Mastercard
Improving Sustainability Efforts With AI
Companies continue to meet the demands of today’s environmentally friendly consumers and can use intelligence to forward a brand’s sustainable purpose. Apple’s new watch is carbon neutral, an innovation-led by design, engineering and operations. The company plans to make all products carbon neutral by 2030 by reducing the three most significant sources of its carbon emissions: electricity, materials and transportation. "Customers are holding brands accountable for the message that companies are putting out in the marketplace, said" Lindsey Scheftic, former CMO of Ring/Amazon
The New CMO
Marketing visionaries and thought leaders at the conference agree that the industry is changing rapidly, and keen marketers who do not want to be left behind need to jump on the rocket. Ideation and creativity, two of the foundational areas of marketing 101, will continue to be where CMOs can add value augmented with AI. Content development and infinite market segmentation will run at warp speed; the question is, are CMOs ready?

title: Will HDD Shortages Slow AI Training And Implementation?
text:
HDDs store the majority of the world’s information, particularly in data centers, but HDDs, like other storage (and memory) technologies have experienced a significant decline in demand during much of 2022 and in 2023 so far. This is largely because large data centers and enterprise customers bought more storage products than they needed at the time during the supply chain crisis in the COVID pandemic. As a consequence, HDD and SSD company stocks have suffered. HDD companies have cut back on production and laid employees off as demand slackened.
Finis Conner was one of the founders of Seagate Technology back in 1979 and he has been a founder of several other digital storage ventures since then. He is one of the pioneers in modern storage technologies. He recently wrote a blog in LinkedIn on a likely disparity between the demand for digital storage and particularly hard disk drives, in order to support data intensive activities such as AI training, and the availability of these storage devices after an extended period of low demand.
AI requires lots of processors to train models but the data used for training will likely live on SSDs as primary storage for data being actively processed but with HDDs as the inexpensive storage that stores the bulk of this data until required for processing. After an extended period of low demand resulting in cutbacks in production and employment, a sudden increase in demand for storage could quickly wipe out any excess in the industry and could lead to shortages that might hobble efforts to ramp up new AI models until storage producers could hire the workers, restart idled production lines and get their factories running at full speed again. This is particularly a problem for hard disk drives.
The article points out that major cloud storage (hyperscale data center) companies such as Google, Microsoft, Meta and AWS are spending billions of dollars building new data centers. Finis points out the likely storage bottleneck in implementing these new AI workflows. “On one level, it’s connected to an HDD supply surplus from the pandemic. On a more concerning level, it brings the potential for an HDD supply crisis that could, temporarily, bring trillion-dollar companies to their knees.”
A Fortune Business Insights article projects that the global data storage market is expected to grow from $247.32B in 2023 to $777.98B by 2030. Despite this projected growth HDD company stocks are down considerably from their 2022 highs. Seagate is down by 48%, Western Digital is down by 32% as is Toshiba. These companies have responded by lowing their production capacity and reducing personnel to reduce their costs, but lowering production capacity, immediately before the AI data storage demand tsunami strikes creates a dangerous situation.
Conner says that “it will take a lot of time to start the HDD production engine back up again. While it’s true that HDD orders are retreating, the wave of AI—and its demand for data storage—is growing by orders of magnitude, and so is its ravenous hunger for data. It reminds me of a tsunami, and right now the disk drive industry is seeing the waters pull back, and wondering why. My serious question is, will the three HDD makers be ready for it when the tide eventually turns, and the big wave hits?”
There are signs that these shortages may be starting to impact industry. The article says that last month Toyota unexpectedly stopped production at 28 assembly lines in 14 Japanese auto plants because “an error occurred due to insufficient disk space, causing the system to stop.”
To show this demand, Finis referenced a chart from an August 2023 blog by this author, shown below. AI and other big data analysis will drive demand for all storage devices, including HDDs. This will be served by shipping higher capacity HDDs, but that alone is not enough to meet capacity demand and the total number of HDDs shipped for enterprise and data center applications will need to increase.
There are currently three HDD companies, but it is possible that this number could decline to two companies in the coming months as Toshiba is acquired in a $14B deal that will take the company private and perhaps get rid of currently low or non-profitable businesses such as its HDD division. This could further restrain the supply of HDDs.
All these factors led Finis to speculate that HDD companies are undervalued. “These mergers and acquisitions in the HDD sector are timely. They show change is already in process. But more than that, consider the roughly $40 billion value of the three HDD manufacturers and compare it to the value of the cloud data storage businesses of Apple, Google, and AWS combined. That’s over $6 trillion. These numbers don’t add up to the enabling value HDD suppliers bring to the table. It seems like nobody is paying attention to the importance of these companies—and the overall fragility of the HDD supply chain.”
Finis points out that this creates a potential opportunity for HDD companies. If they can equip themselves to ramp up production and make supply chains more resilient, they may be able to help meet this imminent and growing demand for storage. He thinks one way to do this is to bring some production back to the US, similar to current semiconductor reshoring efforts.
My own take is that demand for storage driven by AI and other processing trends will likely use up the excess HDD inventory by the end of 2023 and that we will see significant growth in demand for HDDs in 2024 and future years to support the widespread training and utilization of AI models and other big data processing tasks.
HDD pioneer, Finis Conner, believes that HDD companies may be undervalued and that demand for digital storage to support the training and use of AI models which will transform all aspects of business and work could be hampered by shortages in the near future.

title: Council Post: Adapt Or Persist? Analyzing 5 B2B Marketing Trends In 2023
text:
Sean Shea is a philanthropist, TEDx speaker and founder and CEO of ViB, a company that generates quality leads for B2B companies globally.
The marketing landscape is undergoing a significant shake-up—from a laser focus on data privacy to widespread layoffs in tech to the game-changing impact of generative AI. When it comes to marketing strategies, it’s crucial to understand what’s shifted and what’s remained constant.
Recently, my company surveyed more than 300 B2B marketing professionals with the goal of understanding their priorities and budgets, as well as how they’re using AI. Based on our findings, I’ve identified five trends and strategies for business leaders and marketers as we venture further into the back half of 2023.
1. There’s Room To Optimize The Middle And Bottom-Of-Funnel
One thing we’re trending positively toward is meeting and exceeding our lead targets for the top-of-funnel: 77% of B2B marketers were on target in terms of generating basic contact information from new leads. However, nearly a quarter of organizations fell well below their conversion rate targets when it came to qualifying leads and ultimately acquiring customers. A staggering 25% of organizations were under targets in generating meetings for sales, and 24% fell below targets in generating marketing-sourced revenue. In other words, there’s a lot of work to be done regarding the entire sales funnel, particularly the middle and bottom-of-funnel.
While data aggregation and web crawling tools have simplified lead generation near the top of the funnel, teams now face the challenge of optimizing conversions. You can do this by enhancing targeted lead nurturing, utilizing account-based marketing and remarketing strategies and focusing on generating more qualified leads (more on this in a minute).
2. You Can Do More With Less To Maximize Your Content’s Impact
We found that 53% of marketers are focused on repurposing content this year as a smart resource allocation strategy. By efficiently utilizing existing content, whether through revising older pieces or condensing long-form copy into bite-sized blogs, videos or other formats, marketers can create content for multiple channels from a single source.
Repurposing content isn’t a novel concept but, the way I see it, it’s a trend that aligns seamlessly with our current macroeconomic climate. Repurposing content not only saves time and effort in content creation but also allows marketers to adapt their messaging to different formats, catering to the preferences of their audience or platform. Creating a standard operating procedure for this process can help simplify and standardize your content repurposing strategy, while also improving your efficiency.
3. Embrace Generative AI With Caution
When it comes to the latest newcomer—generative artificial intelligence—adaptation is crucial. Of the marketers we talked to, 85% see AI as having a positive impact on B2B marketing in the next 12 months, with generative AI having the most impact on content marketing. Yet, only 38% of marketers have formalized plans to use AI within the next 12 months.
The most striking thing about these findings is that marketers see both the massive potential and the high risks involved: 59% of B2B marketers are concerned about the quality of AI-generated materials. Other concerns include data privacy and security, as well as AI bias, ethics and discrimination.
This is new territory we’re traversing, so I recommend embracing it but doing so carefully. If you can improve efficiency without putting out poor-quality, brand-damaging content or losing sight of the fundamentals, there’s definitely room to maximize the capabilities of generative AI right now ahead of your competitors.
4. Brand Awareness Has Never Been More Important
In surveying B2B marketers, we gave them a list of marketing priorities and asked them to choose three. A notable 51% of marketers chose “Brand Awareness” as a top priority in 2023. In other words, branding cannot be taken lightly or considered an afterthought.
To me, investing in brand building has incredible spillover effects on every tenet of your business—market differentiation, customer trust and loyalty and resilience in times of uncertainty. I believe being persistent with strategic brand building, even if it doesn’t always have direct ROI, is key for sustainable success in the years to come.
5. Don’t Forget The Basics Of Lead Generation
Lead generation stood out as a significant theme. The top challenges reported by marketers were enhancing lead quality and conversion rates (54%) and increasing lead volume (41%). Interestingly, the key marketing priorities aligned with these challenges, with 49% emphasizing generating more leads and 46% focusing on improving lead quality and conversion rates.
Here’s the thing: The basics never change, and they should never be forgotten in light of more advanced marketing tactics. The fundamentals are still about having a clearly defined target audience, a compelling value proposition and an effective lead capture and conversion process, to name a few. Whether you’re newer to B2B marketing or highly experienced, there’s nothing better than revisiting the fundamentals to lay a solid foundation for success.
Staying Ahead Of The Curve In 2023
We’re just getting started on a transformative journey, and now is an opportune moment to reassess strategies and embrace innovative approaches. The key is to do so without forgetting the fundamentals, ensuring you stay ahead of the curve in this ever-evolving B2B marketing landscape. With the right strategies in place, success awaits in the dynamic world of B2B marketing in 2023 and beyond.

title: Council Post: Four Lessons Learned From The Evolution Of AI
text:
Eric Vermillion is the CEO of Helpshift.
It seems like new AI technology is springing up overnight and making massive leaps forward faster than the rest of the world can keep up. Companies are scrambling to invest in AI solutions. AI enthusiasts are quick to proclaim that AI is going to change everything. But I believe a lot of this hype is premature or misdirected.
AI is not a superhuman force that’s going to magically transform the world. The truth is that AI is not "new." Companies have been developing AI tools and chatbots for years. And just like the evolution of any new technology, the development of AI has brought some successes and failures along the way.
Let's look at some lessons learned from the evolution of AI and consider how today’s business leaders can make smarter AI investments.
1. Ignore the hype and focus on the problem.
There has been a lot of hype recently about AI, and while this hype is justified based on the amazing advances we have seen, in the end, AI is a tool for us humans to use to solve problems. We have seen the hype cycle before. For example, back in 2011, IBM’s Watson AI technology was heavily hyped, defeated Jeopardy champion Ken Jennings, and was named “Person of the Year” at the Webby Awards. Articles were written about how soon Watson would be replacing human lawyers. After the hype died down, IBM’s AI technology continued to develop and has helped serve millions of customers by being folded into other tech solutions over the years.
The lesson is that it is not about the hype but the problems that can be solved. This next generation of AI is extremely powerful. It's pre-trained with powerful language models, has extensive real-world knowledge and comes with a very low barrier to entry. Brands that ignore the hype and instead focus on their problems will quickly see where AI can assist in making our lives easier and better. This is especially true when it comes to AI-based customer experience (CX) and AI assistants. I expect that the current AI hype cycle will die down, but AI will be infused into the background, enhancing existing processes and solving problems.
2. Approach AI from a practical perspective.
It seems like every company right now is announcing new investments and initiatives for AI. But this often feels frantic and a little desperate, like people are just trying to tack on “AI” to their company, even if it doesn’t fit.
My company has been working with AI for several years, but we try to take a holistic approach, not just implement AI for AI’s sake. Before your company invests in a big-splash AI initiative, take a step back and ask, “How can this really help solve a customer problem?”
For example, in the customer service and CX industry, lots of companies are excited about using AI for customer service. But one thing we’re discovering is that some companies don’t want “too much” AI or automation in their CX solutions. They want their customer service to sound human and authentic, not uncanny or robotic. In many instances like these, AI is used best as a “sidekick” for human workers, not a replacement. AI solutions can be massively helpful for specific problems like segmenting customers, recognizing customer requests and supporting customers with self-service for routine inquiries. But we still need the human element.
3. Treat AI like you would treat a human co-worker.
Companies are experimenting with popular generic generative AI models in a number of ways to help their workforce. However, it is important to understand that these models, although very powerful, are trained to be generalists based on a general knowledge of language and a vast set of public information. They can be good at answering questions or providing general insight, but without specialized training, guidance or process rules, they will be limited in what they can do.
Just like a newly hired human employee comes with a lifetime of experience, in order to make them effective, organizations need to take the time to train and provide processes or guides to their human employees. In the same way, generative AI should be augmented with brand-specific training, rules and processes. With proper training and guidance, AI can become a specialist with real power to solve unique problems.
4. AI is not the answer to everything.
Lots of companies are taking the attitude that AI is the "next big thing." But AI can’t do everything. Leverage AI where it makes sense, integrate AI into non-AI areas where it adds value, but don’t expect AI to be the entire focus of your tech or business operations.
It’s OK to have menus, it’s OK to have some manual features and it’s OK to have non-AI technology working alongside the AI technology. AI doesn’t belong in every workflow or customer conversation.
For example, AI can be used for automated customer service to help analyze a customer’s intent when starting a conversation. If a customer types into the chatbot, “I want my money back,” the AI can help categorize the request and start the refund process. However, if you add a simple menu in the chat UI offering the top customer service requests to start the conversation, such as "Request Refund," often customers simply will choose from the menu. The menu may not be "AI," but combining AI with non-AI elements (like a menu) can lead to extremely high intent classification.
I believe in the power of AI and automation to boost productivity and help people do more of what they do best. However, business leaders must think carefully and strategically about when and how to build AI solutions into their work processes and customer conversations. Don’t get so dazzled by AI’s bright future that you lose sight of why it’s useful and how to leverage it practically.

title: Council Post: Unlock AI’s Potential: 18 Creative Strategies For Comms Teams
text:
Artificial intelligence—including generative AI such as ChatGPT—is on every company’s radar at this point, and leaders and professionals across teams and specialties are looking into leveraging it to speed up processes and free up time for high-impact projects. With work that’s heavily focused on messaging and team and client support, communications professionals in particular have good reason to dig into its possibilities.
From sparking ideas to refining drafts to researching target audiences, AI can be an incredibly valuable tool for comms teams. Below, experts from Forbes Communications Council discuss ways they and their teams are applying AI to streamline and support a variety of essential everyday tasks.
1. Summarize Article Takeaways
When attention spans are increasingly shrinking, brevity is your friend. Utilizing ChatGPT to summarize a takeaway from a long-form article or consolidate messaging are just two examples of ways to use AI to ensure your comms team delivers relevant, brief and to-the-point messaging. - Sherri Schwartz, OvationCXM
2. Create Copy And Other Content Assets
AI itself—and its application in marketing functions—is not new. Take the example of content creation: The ability to implement machine translation engines (trained or not trained) has been around for a while. Generative AI, however, opens up new opportunities, including summarizing competitive insights, analyzing brand sentiment and, of course, the much-discussed creation of copy and assets. - Nina Etienne, SumUp

3. Analyze Audiences’ Reactions To Your Messaging
Consider using AI for sentiment analysis that your company can leverage to see how various audiences are reacting to your messaging. With sentiment analysis, you can understand positive and negative reactions as well as the tone that is set by your communications. - Roshni Wijayasinha, Prosh Marketing
4. Repurpose Thought Leadership Content
Use AI to keep your team focused on crafting unique ideas, beautiful phrasing and impact-oriented strategy plans; outsource everything else as much as possible. For example, use tools to iterate on core content. If you write an in-depth thought leadership article, you can use ChatGPT to create versions that shift the emphasis slightly for each of your customer personas—along with 50 social posts and sample sales emails to boot! - Leslie Lee, Vistar Media
5. Pull Key Points From News Bulletins
Many companies send out internal comms with weekly or even daily lists of competitors in the news. These articles are often links that cover great information about your competitors, but it’s tough to find time to read through all of them regularly. Use ChatGPT to provide bulleted summaries (no more than three to five top points) that you can distribute along with the links. - Rekha Thomas, Path Forward Marketing LLC
6. Analyze Data
While AI has been around for a very long time and has been used in phones, cars and robots, ChatGPT recently made it a household name, and at our company, we’ve found that ChatGPT is accurate. We use it to analyze data, primarily to see if we may have missed any critical points. I still believe the best responses any AI tool generates are based on the prompts used by us. So, yes, it’s still human-focused, and we need to know what to ask. - Parna Sarkar-Basu, Brand and Buzz Marketing, LLC.
7. Match Titles And Summaries With Keywords And Topics
One thing internal authors sometimes struggle with (especially subject matter experts who aren’t professional communicators) is a lack of understanding about the discoverability of intranet pages. AI functionality makes it easy to match titles and summaries with metadata such as keywords and topics. This increases the likelihood of the page answering queries with a high degree of relevance. - Scott Hitchins, Interact Software
8. Monitor Online Articles About Your Company And Industry
Use AI to continuously scan, analyze and categorize news articles, social media posts, blogs and other public communications related to your company, its products, competitors and the industry. Beyond just identifying mentions, AI can assess the sentiment of the content, determine its potential impact and even predict future trends or potential PR crises. - Ryan Becnel, Energea
9. Research Your Target Customers
MarComms teams can use AI tools such as ChatGPT to gather research on target customers. Try asking ChatGPT to give you information about your core customer’s behavior, preferences and trends to optimize your targeting strategy. You can build thoughtful customer profiles and personas by gathering information on customer buying behavior, social media interactions and more. - Vince Venditti, American Residential Services
10. Strengthen Your Brand Voice
Integrating AI such as ChatGPT into a comms team can revolutionize real-time content optimization. As the team drafts messages or campaigns, AI can instantly analyze language for clarity, tone and target audience resonance, suggesting refinements to maximize impact and ensuring a consistent brand voice across channels. - Jonathan Shroyer, Arise Gaming
11. Filter Search Results
AI can be used to filter through the vast amount of conversations happening online to identify those that are relevant to your business. This can be done by using natural language processing to analyze the content of conversations and identify keywords and phrases so you can then focus your attention on them and take action as needed. - Cade Collister, Metova
12. Supplement And Support Brainstorming Sessions
AI can be a great tool for brainstorming and ideation. Consider having ChatGPT “attend” your next brainstorming session and having someone prompt it for ideas throughout the meeting. Leverage AI to bring outside-the-box ideas to the group, since it has no fear of offering up a potentially controversial or “bad” idea. Then use those ideas to drive ideation in new directions. - Tom Wozniak, OPTIZMO Technologies, LLC
13. Offload Mundane Tasks
All comms teams should explore how AI tools such as ChatGPT can take on mundane tasks. Ask your team to shift how they approach to-do lists, and encourage them to take advantage of this new assistant to free up time to focus on high-impact projects. For example, AI can help synthesize activity tracking for internal reporting or manage deliverables across channels. - Dayle Hall, SnapLogic
14. Use It As An Editor
AI has the potential to transform the communication landscape, but the professionals behind the screen are irreplaceable. AI can be a great tool for crafting and refining a message. Think of ChatGPT as an editor, helping writers form an even stronger response. This tool gives teams a starting point to help spark creativity, guiding them in the right direction to elevate the content from there. - Jonathan Kaufman, Sage Dental
15. Generate Images And Optimize Communications
We have integrated Midjourney for image generation, accelerating design workflows and fostering innovation. We also leverage ChatGPT to craft and enhance textual content, optimizing communication. - Jorge Lukowski, NEORIS
16. Create Personalized Responses To Inquiries
AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT can revolutionize content creation for communication teams. By using previous interactions and brand standards, AI can generate personalized responses for customer inquiries on social media platforms, improving engagement and support. - Antony Robinson, Novalnet AG
17. Analyze Past Content To Generate New Content
By analyzing past content, AI tools can suggest social media posts or draft blogs. Communications team members can then edit and approve the drafts, saving time. As AI learns what resonates, it optimizes content. With human oversight, AI handles the initial head start and increases efficiency. - Sowmya Moni, Incture
18. Turn Spoken Thoughts Into Ready-To-Use Content
Use the power of voice. Oasis is a favorite tool of mine—you speak a stream of consciousness aloud, and its AI platform turns it into a variety of ready-to-use formats, including tweets, press articles and video scripts. Idea generation is hard enough when you’re sitting down to write, so why not talk it out when an idea pops into your head? - Patrick Ward, Formula.Monks

title: Council Post: AI In Mining: The Ten Pillars Of Trust
text:
Founder and CEO at IntelliSense.io. Using AI to help miners increase their net metal supply and enable our clean energy future.
The many challenges of integrating technology into mining processes are well understood. These same challenges make the implementation of AI particularly daunting, resulting in numerous attempts but limited successes.
The mining industry, for example, faces the unique challenge of working with ever-changing inputs due to the dynamic nature of the operating landscape. Unlike other industries—like manufacturing with stable assembly line inputs—mining deals with fluctuating ore properties and changing operating conditions that demand distinct processing strategies for optimal mineral recovery.
Because of this, practical examples of AI triumphs in the mining sector remain somewhat rare, especially where AI technology is being used by front-line operators in shift-oriented decision-making in real time.
With the above considerations in mind, I will outline the core pillars required to make AI deployments a success in mining. The value to be unlocked is vast, but there are clear pitfalls that need to be well understood and carefully navigated.
1. Industry-Specific AI
Be sure to adopt an approach that has been designed for the unique and complex challenges peculiar to mining, including the need for insights to be delivered in real time, variance in the ore feed, low data quality and the need to take into consideration the physical properties of the underlying process and the specific equipment.
2. Real-time Digital Twins
Immediate, real-time results—specifically predictions—are imperative. Hindsight isn't an option. Start with real-time digital twins of unit processes and equipment to deliver hidden insights that are critical for better operational decision-making.
3. Scientific AI
The AI approach that is most suited to the rigors of the mining industry features the fusion of mechanistic (first principle/physics) models with machine learning techniques to deliver target outputs from the process while operating within the constraints of the real world or laws of physics.
4. Engaging Users
Gaining user trust requires transparency and the "explainability" of the AI’s thought process. Trust should be further developed by allowing users to influence the AI outputs through the choice of "value drivers" (e.g., allowing them to optimize for throughput, recovery, energy, water or a combination).
5. Robust, Scalable And Secure
This only comes from the ability to expose the AI solution to learn from diverse scenarios, including multiple ore bodies, geographies and commodities. This ensures that models developed across commodities and sites provide unmatched expertise with transfer learning built in.
6. Simulation And Testing Of Outcomes
Allowing operators to test AI predictions and simulate outcomes also reinforces trust. Providing operations with the option to evaluate “lost opportunity” by seamlessly reaching back in time to evaluate what the AI would have recommended compared to what happened, likewise, further deepens user trust.
7. Explainable AI
Trust comes from knowing the AI will tell you if it’s unsure of the outputs and allow operators to override with confidence. This means you must adopt the fundamentals of data uncertainty when developing AI and factor that into the model.
8. Delivering Sustainable AI Change
Making AI "stick" for the long haul requires embedding AI into the current workflows. This will improve its output and build trust between the technology and the end user.
There is often a failure to recognize that this new breed of AI applications relies on continuously calibrated models and learns further with human feedback. It also requires users to engage with the AI to override the technology and provide feedback to the model outputs.
This is only possible by embedding the technology in user workflows, mapping the technology outputs to user roles and ensuring the technology understands the user’s job well. Unlike previous generations of software, AI is not something that can be built, implemented and then left alone. This is a new and very different approach to that required of the old traditional software world.
9. Data And Outputs: The Only Intellectual Property That Matters
AI is no different than the cloud computing and "rentable" software revolution of the last two decades: It will become a utility that will permeate augmenting all human actions in the world going forward.
There is also little real benefit to building and owning the real-time software stack, and it brings a high risk of failure. The real value comes from owning the data—and making your data more robust and complete—while using the outputs to deliver sustaining process improvements.
These continuous predictions and recommendations can deliver sustainable value, and trust is ultimately derived from the value delivered using technology over the longer term and not from a single point in time only.
10. Continuous Innovation
Not only do the outputs require constant attention to ensure accuracy, but the system also needs to be updated and kept current, reflecting mine-site operational changes. Ongoing updates and innovation maintain high-value delivery and superior operator engagement.
Trusting The AI Revolution
The imperative to adopt AI and real-time digital twins in mining is undeniable. In the end, though, it's not just about embracing change; it's about demonstrating its tangible value sustainably over a longer term. It's about building trust and becoming a beacon of transformation for an industry that urgently requires a technological revolution to meet the future demands of an electrified world.

title: Council Post: It Is The Age Of GenAI, But Has It Come Of Age?
text:
Vineet Arora, CTO, and Co-Founder of WinWire brings over 24 years of experience in the IT Services Industry.
What connects the tasks of decoding human DNA, composing timeless symphonies and creating groundbreaking architectural designs? The surprising answer is generative AI (GenAI).
Just a few years back, artificial intelligence (AI) resembled that brilliant but introverted person who sat in the corner of our offices crunching numbers and offering insights. AI has since undergone quite a transformation, acquiring an education that rivals top-tier institutions. It's become an active contributor to research and development, playing a significant role in shaping businesses on a global scale. It's like watching a prodigy blow everyone away at a talent show.
Thanks to impressive advancements such as GPT-4 and DALL-E, AI is no longer limited to just analyzing data; it's creating it. We've undoubtedly entered a new technological phase—the age of GenAI.
However, what will it take to realize the true potential of this technology?
How Did We Arrive At This Point?
Let's examine where we stand today. We are witnessing a significant leap in AI implementation across the board. GenAI is more than just a minor upgrade to AI technologies; it's a paradigm shift. Imagine transitioning from a black-and-white TV to a 4K Ultra-HD experience overnight. We're not discussing AI that merely dissects data or makes predictions; we're talking about AI that can imagine and create. It can compose compelling text, design visuals, and contribute to research and development efforts.
This milestone didn't magically appear out of nowhere. There's an intricate orchestration at play here that's often overlooked. Think about the tireless innovation of researchers and developers, the ethical guidelines that have steered this progress and the considerable financial commitment required to bring us to this stage. These aspects aren't trivial; they form the solid foundation for this transformative technology.
If you're wondering whether the hype surrounding GenAI in the media is justified, allow me to be clear: It is. If you still need to embrace this reality, now is the time to recalibrate your strategic perspective.
GenAI For All: Adapt Or Customize
The days of GenAI being reserved for a privileged few due to high costs or limited access are long gone. Today, whether you're steering a Fortune 500 conglomerate or a burgeoning startup, GenAI is within your reach. The need for an army of data scientists is a thing of the past. AI-as-a-service (AIaaS) platforms level the playing field, offering off-the-shelf solutions and customization options. The question isn't whether you can afford to adopt AI but whether you can afford not to.
Shifting Technological, Regulatory And Business Landscapes
As is typical with emerging technologies, challenges abound. Regulations are playing catch-up, ethical concerns are gaining traction, and the competitive landscape is changing at a breakneck pace. What once took decades during the industrial era is now happening within the age of GenAI in a matter of months.
Let's not forget data privacy and security. The potency of GenAI's creations heavily relies on the data it processes. Striking a balance between ethical use and safeguarding data is a delicate endeavor for governments and organizations.
Embrace The GenAI Era: Six Key Adoption Principles
1. Prioritize core objectives. Focus on how GenAI can drive your core business objectives without getting lost in superficial features.
2. Invest in talent. Hire individuals who understand the AI landscape and speak the language of your industry.
3. Safeguard data integrity. The effectiveness of your AI system hinges on the quality of the data it consumes. Don't make compromises here.
4. Forge intelligent partnerships. Collaborate with entities that can enhance your capabilities through cloud solutions or specialized AI platforms.
5. Uphold ethical standards. Ethics are a must. Establish robust ethical guidelines for AI usage regardless of whether you're creating or adopting the technology.
6. Adapt continuously. This landscape changes rapidly. Evolving your strategies is essential; standing still is not an option.
Speeding Toward A Smarter Tomorrow
Is it the age of GenAI? Unquestionably. Has it fully come of age? Well, that's the billion-dollar question.
My take is that while it's graduated and ready for the job market, it's yet to reach its zenith. We're at a pivotal moment—an opportunity disguised as a challenge. As business leaders, adapting and leading this digital transformation is our prerequisite.
We are not bystanders in this new era; we are the architects. We're in for an exhilarating ride. Adaptation is an existential imperative, and we need to lead rather than simply move with the times. After all, this is not just the age of GenAI; it's the age of limitless possibilities.
Strap in. The future isn't just happening to us. We're actively creating it.

When it comes to what you’re putting on your skin, reports show that consumers not only want the best ingredients, but ones that are ethically-sourced.
That’s why Anisha Gupta, 2022 Under 30 Social Impact lister and cofounder of software platform Bluebird Climate, is in the business of helping beauty and wellness brands go green.
With $3 million in funding, Gupta has devised an AI-backed software that can assess the sustainable life cycle of a product—from how many emissions are emitted in sourcing ingredients to its landfill impact. Bluebird launched in 2021 with cult-favorite beauty brand Glossier as its first client and, over the past six months, has tripled its clientele to a roster of 150 brands, including skincare companies like Hailey Bieber’s Rhode, Glow Recipe, and most recently, Summer Fridays.
Last week, Bluebird announced a partnership with non-profit Pact Collective–which focuses on making beauty and wellness packaging more sustainable–to help brands communicate product recycling instructions directly to consumers through an interactive map based on location, which can be integrated into their e-commerce websites.
Bluebird’s growth this year follows a growing trend: In a 2023 Growing Sustainable Beauty Trends report by NielsenIQ, 45% of surveyed consumers ranked responsible sourcing of beauty products as one of the most important sustainability claims. The study also notes a shift in major retailers like Sephora and Target pushing for environmentally friendly partners, making sustainability a leading trend in the beauty industry.
“It's table stakes for brands today to have a stance around sustainability,” says Gupta, who previously worked in research and development roles at Unilever. “It’s really just making sure that they're not falling behind when it comes to what consumers are expecting of them, and being able to talk about sustainability in a transparent way.”
Bluebird’s clients pay $100 or more per month to grab sustainability data for their products. In many cases, clients aren’t using the data just to scrutinize or improve their practices, but for marketing purposes. Skincare company Versed, for example, includes the statistics alongside each product on their website through Bluebird’s plug-in widgets. The widget redirects customers to a detailed report on the product’s climate and waste impact.
The company also works with a network of eco-friendly suppliers to offer brands new vendors that can help reduce their footprint—which Gupta admits can be tricky business.
Still, the goal isn’t to just be a back-end data provider, Gupta says. The additional tooling is designed to give brands actionable ways to build credibility with their consumers, and to get one step closer to solving the massive waste problem in the industry.

Dubbed the “Million-Dollar Mime,” Khaby Lame has amassed more than 244 million followers across social media platforms without saying a single word in his viral videos. Lame, a 2022 Forbes Under 30 Europe lister, went from assembling car filters in a factory to making silly reaction videos during the pandemic and becoming the world’s most followed person on TikTok. To get him to feature a product on both TikTok and Instagram could cost brands about $750,000. Lame was ranked No. 11 in the 2023 Forbes Top Creators List that launched on Tuesday.

The union of 11,500 screenwriters will start their vote to ratify a new three-year contract on Monday. The parties reached agreements on issues across minimum staffing, residual payments and, of course, artificial intelligence. As of the tentative agreement, studios cannot use AI to rewrite original material, nor force writers to use the tech. Meanwhile, the Actors Guild is still on the picket lines. (The New York Times)
-ChatGPT, it’s just like us! Meta is coming out with chatbots with distinct personalities—like “a sassy robot [that] taps into the type of farcical humor that is resonating with young people,” in order to attract young users to Meta apps. Think this will work with Gen Z? (The Wall Street Journal)
-Known for its farm-fresh ingredients, Sweetgreen’s next endeavor is getting a bit unnatural. Earlier this year, the fast-casual salad company launched a robotic salad assembler at its first “Infinite Kitchen” concept location, where customers order at a kiosk and have their salad made by robotic dispensers. According to Nicolas Jammet, the cofounder and Under 30 2012 Food & Wine lister, the tech will help in “re-deploying [their] team members to be more focused on hospitality and on prepping fresh vegetables.” Will this get them out of their post-pandemic slump? (Forbes)
Venture View
Time to take a look inside the world of venture capital.
This week, we sat down with Amber Illig, a solo general partner at venture capital fund The Council, who invests in early-stage founders. She built her career on the operations teams of brands like Apple, Snap and Cruise before entering the investment industry. Today, her investments focus on pre-seed and seed raises into brands that are innovating on outdated industries, like healthcare, transportation and agriculture.
The following responses have been slightly edited for length and clarity.
What are some trends you’re noticing in venture capital today? Things like healthcare, logistics, manufacturing, supply chain, agriculture are all these areas that we rely on as human beings, but they sometimes don't get as much attention when it comes to VC dollars or tech talent. Interestingly enough, one of the trends that I'm seeing is people are starting to get more excited about those industries right now. We've been through so many hype cycles back to back that people are realizing these industries are recession proof, they're massive markets and all together, they represent 50% of the U.S. GDP.
Are there any challenges you’ve noticed in these industries, specifically? They can be really operationally complex, which makes it tough to have enough insight into them. Plus, they’re not as glamorous. For someone to want to build in these spaces, it takes a specific type of founder.
What’s been the biggest change in venture capital funding over the last year? Investors have just gotten less risky, which is strange because venture capital is by definition a highly risky business. Personally, I love investing at pre-seed and sometimes even pre-revenue if it's the right founder. But the list of people that I can share deals with who will also invest at that stage and co-invest with me is getting smaller and smaller. So one thing I would say is if you're gearing up to raise your first round ever, you may want to start with friends and family rounds.
If founders don’t have wealthy friends and family, what would you suggest their first step be toward those early-stage rounds? Figure out how to break into angel groups and understand and connect with angel investors. There are also several venture firms that like getting in that early— like The Council Fund, Underdog Labs and 43.io.
What is an industry or business type at the top of investors’ minds today? The whole AI craze is ongoing, and that's creating a lot of hype and a lot of people raising capital there. Even non-AI companies are spinning AI into what they're building. But I think investors are also nervous about generative AI because they want to ensure what a founder is building isn’t just adding something on top of chatGPT and calling it differentiated.
What I actually like to see is the companies that are AI second, not AI first. So those that solve a real problem in the world, and then solve it faster and more efficiently by incorporating AI.
What is the biggest opportunity you see for young founders today? We have so many spaces in the United States and in the world that have been historically ignored, but they're absolutely existential. There are problems with the climate, there are problems with healthcare, there are problems with supply chain. There's no shortage of big problems to be solved, so it’s about finding which one you resonate with and which one you have enough experience or insights into to be successful.

title: Apple’s Tim Cook Talks About AI, Apps, Vision Pro And iPhone Gaming
text:
On a speedy visit to London, Apple CEO Tim Cook checked in with three app developers before sitting down to talk to me about where the company is going.
Cook was as effortlessly charismatic as ever, putting the developers at their ease and then answering every question I threw at him with intelligent and thoughtful answers.
He even talked about artificial intelligence, something the company has been relatively quiet about in the past. I asked him about this reticence, comparing it to other companies that never shut up about AI. Does that mean Apple isn’t getting involved with it?
Cook said, “We use AI in our products today fairly pervasively. If you think about the Watch, it's a part of AI that detects whether a fall occurs. It's AI, that detects AFib, it's AI that detects a crash. If you're typing, it's AI that's predicting the next word. And so, there's great uses of AI all over the place. We don't label it as such. We label it as the consumer benefit of fall detection or an ECG or AFib detection, not ‘powered by AI’ or whatever.”
Cook has previously talked about how technology is intrinsically neither good nor bad. So, how does he feel about generative AI? Surprisingly, since it’s not something Apple talks about, it’s nothing new in Cupertino. Cook said, “We've been working on generative AI for years and have done a lot of research. And we're going to approach it really thoughtfully and think about it deeply, because we're fully aware of the not-good uses that it can have, and the issues around bias and hallucination and so forth. You know, we've never felt an urgency to be first, we’ve always felt an urgency to be best, and that is how we go into this as well.”
The apps presented to Cook were interesting. Save Your Wardrobe, presented by Hasna Kourda, is designed to let users manage their clothes, creating a digital version of what’s in their wardrobe. This can remind you of what you own, so those unworn clothes come back into use. It also encourages repair rather than the discarding of garments and can help users access aftercare services from alterations to upcycling.
Gym Streak from Joseph Mambwe was a fitness app that manages your workout for you. Its creator believes it’s more than that, that at its core, “resilience is a superpower that is available to everyone, along with persistence and the will to keep going.” It uses augmented reality (AR) to create videos where the animated figure demonstrating the exercises appears to be working out in your living room.
And Night Sky by Andy Weekes, demonstrated on the balcony of Apple’s Battersea Power Station offices, was a stunning app which also uses AR to make stars, planets and even the International Space Station appear onscreen as you point your iPhone at the place they are in the sky. It can send reminders and messages so you can share what you see – and even what you can’t – with friends and family. All of the developers praised Apple’s support and the power of the technology. And Andy Weekes spoke about how compelling Vision Pro is for his app, saying he was very excited about it. “So are we,” Cook replied. “We’re seeing some incredible work in development. Getting to use it every night, Cook said he believes even more how remarkable spatial computing is.
Gaming has become increasingly important to Apple, and the latest iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max processor promise great capabilities which can be exploited for gaming purposes. At the mention of the processor, the A17 Pro, Cook was simple: “It’s wicked.”
He went on, “I think there’s significant excitement both in terms of A17 Pro and M3 on the Mac, about our role in gaming, and we’re very serious about it—this is not a hobby for us. It’s something we’re putting all of ourselves out there on. iOS is the best gaming platform that’s out there and we want to keep it the best and just keep taking it to the next level. And our silicon road map really is in a camp by itself, we think.”
That silicon could do even more, of course, if more data was sent to the cloud, but Apple wants to do more on-device. Would it ever risk sacrificing privacy to get more power. Cook said, “No. To us, privacy is a fundamental human right and the atmosphere is such that people’s privacy is being challenged every day and we think privacy is more important today than it was ten years ago. It’s one of the most profound issues of the century. We’re not backing off.”

title: Council Post: Reckoning With The Age Of AI (And Planning For Its Future)
text:
Veronica Buitron is co-founder of the Chicago-based ad automation platform, Chassis.
It's understandable if companies are having a difficult time ironing out a roadmap with respect to AI developments—after all, this is a tectonic shift affecting every industry. Workflows are shifting, job responsibilities are changing, entire departments are being overhauled and some companies will even be put out of business. Consequently, deciding how to plan for the future has never been more elusive.
The bad news is that my crystal ball is currently on the fritz. But as someone who has worked closely alongside artificial intelligence advancements over the past 20 years, the good news is that I've still got a pretty solid idea as to the near future of business operations in the age of AI.
Before we get to that, though, it can help to contextualize some of these advancements that seemed to have cropped up overnight.
AI's Past
Artificial intelligence (AI) is by no means a new technology. While it may have become a major flashpoint in the tech scene within the past decade or so, it's been in development since the '70s. So what's changed? Of course, the capabilities have improved greatly, but the main reason we've seen an explosion in the past year is the level of accessibility.
For nearly the entirety of AI's lifespan, if you wanted access, that meant millions if not billions of dollars and mountains of data that the average company just could not access. Now, these insanely powerful tools have been democratized and put within everyone's reach.
AI's Present
Right now, much of the buzz is around language and media tools, with writers and designers being the main demographics worrying about their future. But drafting a blog post or summarizing an article is only the first iteration.
The ones that we're most familiar with are mostly using the same core algorithms and datasets—with the large majority simply plugging into OpenAI. They're black boxes that even their developers don't fully comprehend. They take shortcuts, they fabricate information and they don't have any shame about it. But I am confident that they are going to get better.
AI's Future
Because the inner workings of this tech are largely uniform, most of these applications lack any sort of specialization, but I expect that we will soon see the market splinter off into more and more specific use cases. And that's when things will get really nutty.
Every job and every industry will be shaken. Finance, accounting, software development—jobs that have been bastions for stability may soon be disrupted along with the rest of us.
Creating An Internal AI Roadmap
There are two main ways in which AI can be leveraged to add value to your company. The first and easiest use case here is to incorporate AI as an assistant that helps increase output. In my company, we encourage every department to research, use and share AI tools to help make our jobs more efficient—whether that’s an exec, a writer, a designer or a developer.
While each of these areas requires direct human oversight to account for potential errors, across the board, the time it takes to complete a given task is drastically reduced through the use of these new language models.
The second opportunity, which is harder to execute but will be critical moving forward, is enabling your product or service with AI. We can (and should) use this incredible technology to improve the user experience, speed up software development, enhance customer support efforts, etc.
Here I strongly, strongly advise you to seek out a reputable firm that has done extensive research. This is for two reasons. One, you don’t want to get burned by someone trying to capitalize on this digital gold rush. And two, many people may not even realize the types of use cases that exist for AI and the ways it can help a company.
Some people may think language models don’t apply to their business, but as we’re finding more and more, that is rarely the case. I believe that those who don't start to incorporate AI into their workflows soon will likely face a steeper learning curve and potentially a huge disadvantage compared to their AI-enabled counterparts.
Creating An External AI Roadmap
Some might recall that there was a much smaller AI boom back around 2017 and 2018. Every application that had an algorithm somewhere in its architecture was suddenly "AI-enabled" tech. We can expect a similar thing to happen this time around.
Many companies will likely rebrand and market themselves as AI companies in order to appear cutting-edge. This, combined with the general lack of understanding of what these language models truly are or how they operate, will require companies large and small to do a sizeable amount of due diligence when purchasing new software.

title: Council Post: Generative AI Poses Risks, But Outright Bans Aren’t The Best Solution
text:
John Sun is the founder and CEO of Spring Labs.
For all the encouragement in the corporate world on how business leaders can strategically leverage generative artificial intelligence, hesitation has been growing as well, with some company leaders increasingly fearing the drawbacks of generative AI— and particularly the data security risks posed by these tools.
In light of these growing concerns, some leaders might decide to ban the use of these AI tools outright. But such a reactionary approach is not necessarily the answer.
How Generative AI Can Exacerbate Data Security Issues
The fears some executives have around data security and generative AI are far from unfounded. These tools pose three main data security risks.
First, there’s the issue of unintended data sharing with AI companies. In April 2023, Writer, an enterprise generative AI platform, surveyed 66 people in director-level positions or higher at organizations with over a thousand employees. A key finding? Forty-six percent of respondents believed “someone in their company may have inadvertently shared corporate data with ChatGPT.” Information employees give AI tools, including customer data and intellectual property, could become the property of the companies behind these tools. For instance, according to legal intelligence website JD Supra, OpenAI’s terms of use “do not provide any protection for confidential information that may be input by a user into ChatGPT.” Moreover, if employees accidentally enter sensitive consumer data into ChatGPT, they may be violating their employer’s privacy policy and may trigger notification requirements under data breach laws such as CCPA or other data privacy laws such as GDPR. An even scarier possibility is technology companies could use this information in data training sets for future models and unintentionally expose customers’ sensitive data to users of these models.
Then there’s the risk of data sharing internally and externally. Of course, at any time, employees could copy and share a company’s data with their colleagues or third parties outside the company. But link sharing capabilities within AI solutions can make it even easier for data to end up in the wrong hands. Notably, per reporting by ZDNET, ChatGPT enables users to “share an entire ChatGPT conversation with anyone even if they don't have an account with the popular AI.” It can be difficult, if not impossible, to control the spread of the data in these links—even with strong data loss prevention strategies and software.
However, company leaders should not solely be concerned about their corporate data when it comes to generative AI. They should also be aware of the intellectual property risks associated with the data these AI tools provide them. As noted by Bloomberg Law, even “with the current iteration of ChatGPT, it is unclear if certain outputs might be a derivative work of underlying copyright material, thus risking a potential infringement claim if the output is subject to copyright protection.” And given various copyright infringement lawsuits against OpenAI and the U.S. Copyright Office’s decision to take public comments about AI and copyright matters, greater legal protections could be handed down to the original creators of works.
Outright Bans: One Possible Solution, But Not The Most Feasible One
Some company leaders will analyze the risks above and decide to ban AI platforms from their companies altogether. In fact, according to research published in August 2023 by AI cybersecurity company BlackBerry, “75% of organizations worldwide are currently implementing or considering bans on ChatGPT and other Generative AI applications within the workplace.” Banning AI is technically a way to deal with security issues, but it’s not the most strategic move. Despite the risks, the reality is that AI can have many benefits.
A significant benefit of AI is that it can bolster productivity. According to a 2023 report by McKinsey, generative AI “could enable labor productivity growth of 0.1 to 0.6 percent annually through 2040, depending on the rate of technology adoption and redeployment of worker time into other activities.” This prediction could be a drastic underestimate, particularly for roles that are highly amenable to AI automation, such as customer service positions. In addition to increasing productivity, companies can use AI in other beneficial ways, including increasing customer engagement and making better decisions. Companies that ban AI risk falling behind competitors who savvily leverage it in these ways and more.
Ways To Mitigate Generative AI’s Data Security Risks
Instead of banning AI, executives can explore other ways to mitigate generative AI’s data security risks.
Installing client-side protections, such as automatically detecting and tokenizing sensitive data before it gets sent to AI platforms, is a great place to start. Various tools on the market allow for both data redaction and reversible tokenization. However, cybersecurity leaders should make sure that any solutions they’re considering secure the data on the client side and do not send any raw data to a central server before processing it. Cybersecurity leaders should also pick a solution that maintains high-quality AI responses; the solution should mask data in a manner that still allows AI models to retain semantic context.
Executives should also explore opening enterprise accounts with AI companies if offered. Jasper AI, for example, released its own enterprise generative AI solution in February 2023, and OpenAI released an enterprise form of ChatGPT in August 2023. Enterprise-grade accounts can come with the promise of specific data privacy protections. However, it’s important for cybersecurity leaders and their legal teams to vet the terms and conditions carefully and ask pointed questions about what the AI company can do with their corporate data, including whether or not it can use the data to train future models.
Employee training is also critical. As with other cybersecurity concerns, one of the best ways executives can safeguard their companies is by routinely training their employees. When employees know their way around AI tools, they’ll be more likely to use them effectively and safely. Unfortunately, many workers haven’t received training on how to leverage AI. In research published in June 2023 by the Boston Consulting Group, for instance, 86% of respondents believed that to “prepare for the new era of AI at work,” they will “need training to sharpen their skills.” Yet, just 14% of frontline employees indicated that they’d “gone through any upskilling training to date, compared with 44% of leaders.”
Navigating any early technology is difficult. But AI is simply too important to ignore. When company leaders do their due diligence to vet AI solutions, they can lower data security risks for their team members and customers. They can also pave the way for better work—and better results.
